name: Liposuction / chin lipo

lead: Liposuction removes localized fat through a thin suction tube (cannula) inserted via small incisions. Under the chin and along the neck, the payoff people want is less submental fullness and a sharper jawline and neck angle, sometimes combined with chin surgery.

The cannula is moved through the fat layer to remove cells, often after fluid with dilute anaesthetic is injected (the tumescent technique) [11]. Removed fat cells do not regrow, though remaining fat cells can enlarge, and reference sources say overall body fat generally returns to its earlier level over months. The neck contour shows once swelling settles. A 2004 randomized study found liposuction did not alter insulin action or coronary risk factors. Evidence specific to submental liposuction comes from small registered studies and clinical practice.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon, often with local anaesthesia and sedation for small areas like the chin, and sometimes alongside a chin implant or neck lift. People wear a compression garment for a period afterward, and swelling takes weeks to settle before the final contour shows.

A 2024 meta-analysis of 39 studies and 29,368 patients found contour deformity (2.35 percent), hyperpigmentation (1.49 percent), seroma (0.65 percent) and haematoma (0.27 percent) among complications [1]. Rarer serious events include deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation and embolism, with risk rising with the volume removed [11]. It is surgery under anaesthesia and should be done by a licensed surgeon.

chain: Fat suctioned from chin and neck
angle.text: Fat is suctioned from under the chin and neck, reducing submental fullness so the jawline and neck angle look sharper. Removed fat cells do not return, and the contour shows once swelling settles.

lead: Liposuction, also called lipoplasty or suction-assisted lipectomy, is a surgical procedure in which fat is removed from beneath the skin by suction through a cannula [1]. Submental (chin) liposuction targets the fat pad under the chin and along the front of the neck. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to make the jawline and the angle between chin and neck read more sharply, because removing the fullness beneath the jaw leaves the bone and neck outline more visible [2][3].

Submental work is usually done through one or two very small incisions, often under local anaesthesia, and may be combined with other procedures such as chin implants, genioplasty, orthognathic surgery or neck lifts [4][5]. Alternatives that people compare it with include injectable fat-dissolving products such as deoxycholic acid (sold as Kybella, approved by the US FDA in 2015 for fat below the chin) and weight loss [6].

Wikipedia reports that the technique was developed in Rome in the mid-1970s by Arpad and Giorgio Fischer, extended to the whole body by Yves-Gérard Illouz and Fournier, and that Jeffrey Klein's tumescent method using dilute lidocaine later enabled procedures under local anaesthesia [1]. In the US it became the most commonly performed cosmetic procedure in 2015 according to the same source [1].

Reference sources say removed fat cells are permanently gone, but that overall body fat generally returns to its earlier level within months, with fat sometimes redistributing to other areas [1]. A 2004 randomized study found that removal of subcutaneous fat by liposuction did not alter insulin action or coronary heart disease risk factors [7]. Research specific to the chin and neck consists of case series, a scoping review and a systematic review of its use alongside jaw surgery [5].

paras: Wikipedia describes several techniques: suction-assisted, tumescent, power-assisted, water-jet assisted, ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted and radiofrequency-assisted liposuction, which surgeons often combine within one session [1]. In the tumescent method a large volume of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine is injected before suction so that the procedure can be done with local anaesthesia [1]. A randomized study compared radiofrequency-assisted liposuction and a helium-based skin-tightening device with VASER-assisted liposuction for arm contouring [8].

For the neck, the technique is typically adapted to a small treatment area. Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, states that narrower cannulas of roughly two to three millimetres are used on delicate areas such as the face and neck [9].

A case series from a French team (Aldihani and colleagues, 2025) reviewed 695 patients treated under local anaesthesia between October 2020 and August 2022. The authors describe the procedure as a minimally invasive option for reducing volume when rejuvenating the face, report complications that were minimal and mainly surface irregularities that responded to massage and ultrasound, and argue it should be offered as a low-drawback option [5].

When submental liposuction is combined with surgery on the jaws, a 2024 systematic review in Annals of Plastic Surgery found ten studies covering 67 patients. All reported cervical aesthetic benefit; complications listed included lower-lip sensory change, facial nerve injury, infection, residual submental fullness and skin irregularities. The authors described the combination as appearing safe but noted that the evidence is limited and not standardised [5].

According to Wikipedia, an early setback came in 1926 in France, when a dancer's leg was amputated after excessive tissue removal and tight suturing, an event that dampened interest in body contouring for decades [1]. In the mid-1970s the Fischers developed a blunt cannula with suction, which they called liposculpture, and in 1977 reviewed 245 cases of cellulite treatment of the hip and thigh area. Illouz developed a wet technique using saline and hyaluronidase, Fournier promoted compression after surgery, and in the 1980s American dermatologists led by Jeffrey Klein developed the tumescent technique [1].

Liposuction became the most commonly performed US cosmetic procedure in 2015, overtaking breast augmentation, according to Wikipedia [1]. The same year the FDA approved deoxycholic acid for reducing fat below the chin, giving submental fat an injectable, non-surgical alternative [6]. Grokipedia, citing American Society of Plastic Surgeons data, gives 349,728 US liposuction procedures in 2024 [9].

Liposuction is used for cosmetic body contouring and for medical indications such as lipedema, lymphedema and lipomas [1]. A systematic review of lipedema treatments found tumescent liposuction had the strongest evidence for sustained symptom improvement, though most studies were observational [10], and a randomized trial protocol compares surgery with decongestive therapy for lipedema [11]. A Danish review of gynaecomastia reports that surgical excision with liposuction can provide excellent results with a low complication rate when the glandular enlargement persists [12].

In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-surgery contexts, submental liposuction is applied to a heavy under-chin region sometimes called a double chin or, on forums, a "neckbeard" fat pad. A poster in one looksmax.org thread said the surgeon removed roughly 20 to 30 ml and that jaw definition emerged as swelling resolved, with a cost of about 1,500 in western Europe [2].
A registered study, NCT04283708, compares chin advancement genioplasty with and without submental liposuction for skeletal chin deficiency [4].

Wikipedia reports that evidence does not support an effect on weight beyond a couple of months, that treated fat cells are permanently removed, and that overall fat generally returns to pre-treatment levels, sometimes in other areas including visceral fat [1]. A randomized study found that liposuction did not change insulin action or risk factors for coronary heart disease [7].

Grokipedia says skin contraction continues over three to six months and that touch-up procedures may be considered in a minority of cases [9]. A 2013 Indian series of more than 600 suction-assisted cases reported under-correction in 5.3 percent and over-correction in 3.7 percent of patients [13].

Grokipedia, summarising guidance attributed to the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, says swelling usually peaks in the first one to two weeks, bruising peaks around seven to ten days, and the final contour appears around three to six months. It adds that compression garments are commonly worn for several weeks and that manual lymphatic drainage massage is sometimes started one to two weeks after surgery [9].

Forum posters describe the same swelling phase. In one looksmax.org thread a user one month after surgery asked whether a lump under the chin would still subside, and other members asked about timelines [14]. The Aldihani series reports that surface irregularities were managed with massage and ultrasound [5].

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 39 studies with 29,368 patients (mean age 40.6, mean BMI 26.4) reported contour deformity at 2.35 percent, hyperpigmentation 1.49 percent, seroma 0.65 percent, haematoma 0.27 percent, superficial burn 0.25 percent and allergic reaction 0.16 percent. Wikipedia describes risk as dependent on volume, listing deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding, infection, fat embolism, lidocaine toxicity and skin necrosis, and cites a 2011 estimate of about one death per 10,000 cases [1]. It also reports that deaths among US citizens after cosmetic surgery abroad, notably in the Dominican Republic between 2009 and 2022, were mostly attributed to embolism [1].

A 2013 review by Dixit and Wagh of unfavourable liposuction outcomes, drawing on more than 600 cases, listed seromas (3.5 percent), surface irregularities (8.2 percent), asymmetry (2.7 percent), skin laxity (4.2 percent) and skin necrosis (1 percent), and noted that a minority of patients were dissatisfied even when surgeons judged results good. The authors recommend screening for unrealistic expectations and body dysmorphic disorder [13].

A 2022 scoping review of complications after submental liposuction screened 539 articles and included four. Reported complications included submental depression, oedema, hypertrophic scarring, scar contracture, cervical necrotizing fasciitis, cervicofacial dystonia and transient facial nerve paralysis; follow-up ranged from three to twelve months. The authors concluded that anatomical knowledge and prompt management are essential [5].

Studies include a 2024 meta-analysis of complications, a randomized metabolic study [7], randomized comparisons of lipedema surgery and conservative therapy [11], an arm-contouring randomized trial [8]. For the face and neck, the evidence consists of the 695-patient local-anaesthesia series, a scoping review of four studies of complications, a systematic review of ten small studies combining submental liposuction with orthognathic surgery, and the registered genioplasty trial [4][5]. No published randomized trial of submental liposuction alone for jawline definition in young men was identified.

Costs vary widely. A looksmax.org poster reported about 1,500 in western Europe for submental lipo [2]. Grokipedia gives a US average around 4,000 dollars for liposuction generally, with advanced techniques costing more, and says destinations abroad are described as 30 to 70 percent cheaper but with added risks [9]. Posters comparing options mention that Turkey is considered affordable for liposuction and that clinic sessions of an injectable fat-dissolver cost roughly 200 to 400 pounds each [3].

On looksmax.org, one poster argues that neck liposuction is a very good surgery for people who are not severely weak-jawed and says the results are permanent [15]. Threads titled around submental lipo results share before-and-after photos, swelling updates and costs [2][14]. Other posts discuss combining liposuction with genioplasty as a lower-risk alternative to double-jaw surgery, comparing it with fat-dissolving injections such as Aqualyx for cheek and jaw fat, and raising concerns about removing too much facial fat [3].

One comparison thread weighs Aqualyx sessions, which the poster notes can be done cheaply but carry reported risks such as nerve damage and skin necrosis when done improperly, against a single surgical procedure; replies advise using a clinic [3]. Members also debate whether leanness is a prerequisite, with one reply asking whether the poster was otherwise lean apart from an unlucky submental deposit [2].

Related approaches include deoxycholic acid injections for submental fat [6], buccal fat removal, chin augmentation or genioplasty, neck lifts and fat loss through diet and training. Posts on forums frequently present these as options at different points on the cost, downtime and invasiveness scale [3].

lore.intro: Submental and neck liposuction is discussed as a durable route to a leaner lower third, with disagreement over how permanent the results are, how it compares with injections, and how much fat is safe to remove [15][2][3].

claims.claim: Liposuction permanently removes fat from the jaw and neck.
Liposuction is a low-risk shortcut compared with dieting.
A small amount of submental fat removal produces a visible jaw upgrade.
Liposuction can be combined with genioplasty instead of bimaxillary surgery for a more defined face.
Fat-dissolving injections are an easier alternative to surgery for facial fat.
The result is final within weeks.
